These could include CCfD, the H2Global and direct subsidies for steel producers (all of which were already in place by the time of this announcement). There is a range of estimates of 0.6-0.9 Mtpa of RFNBO supply needed to satisfy the industry target (see references). Germany said it will recognise the refinery route. It has not signalled plans for a separate multiplier or "correction factor" to lower the value compared with direct use of RFNBOs in mobility
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Tax incentives for hydrogen production
description: Mauritania has introduced a comprehensive incentive framework to attract green hydrogen investments. Key benefits include exemptions from VAT and export taxes, a reduction in import customs duties from 4% to 2% for early projects, and corporate tax incentives. To qualify, operators must be Mauritanian-incorporated companies with proven technical and financial capacity. Projects begin with a framework agreement with the government (valid for up to two years, extendable once), followed by a global agreement outlining development terms. Production licenses are granted for up to 35 years, renewable twice for 10 years each. The law also establishes the Mauritanian Agency for Green Hydrogen (AMHV) to oversee the sector and includes plans to issue guarantees of origin to certify the renewable nature of hydrogen, supporting export ambitions, particularly to Europe.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Tax incentives for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Framework agreement (for land concession)
description: An agreement was signed in February 2025 between the Minister of Energy and Petroleum and the CEO of GreenGo Energy to grant GreenGo Energy access to more than 100000 hectares of land near Nouakchott, Mauritania, to develop the transformative Megaton Moon Green Hydrogen Project. With the agreement, GreenCo Energy enters the development phase of the project. Phase 1 of the project is set for completion by 2029 with a capacity of 500 MW for the electrolyzer, 600 MW for onshore wind, and 600 MW for solar PV to produce nearly 339 ktpa of renewable ammonia. The targeted full capacity of the project is 6 GW of electrolysis, 6.8 GW of onshore wind, and 6.3 GW of solar PV
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Subsidieregeling Waterstof in mobiliteit (SWIM) (Hydrogen in Mobility Subsidy Scheme)
description:
EUR 40 million for zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) and hydrogen refueling stations (HRS) for heavy transport.

HRS conditions:

≥500 kg/day
350 & 750 bar
Public access
100% renewable hydrogen by 2036
Incentives:

Up to 40% of HRS costs (max EUR 2 million)
Up to 80% of ZEV cost difference (max EUR 5 million)
February 2025: 9 of 12 applications approved by RVO, supporting:

192 heavy-duty vehicles
10 passenger vans
9 small hydrogen delivery vans
Next funding round open until May 2025
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: BMDV Alternative Drives in Rail Transport Funding programme (Förderprogramm für alternative Antriebe im Schienenverkehr)
description: Germany allocated €412 million for 2021–2026 to support alternative drive technologies in rail transport, including hydrogen. Funding covers up to 50% for studies and analyses, 45% for electrolysis, 50% for hydrogen refueling stations (HRS), and 40% for the procurement or conversion of rail vehicles. Separate applications are required for each funding component. Three funding rounds have been completed: €87 million in February 2021, €141 million in August 2022, and €93 million in June 2023.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Funding Programme for FCEVs "KSNI-Förderprogramm"
description: Germany has allocated €2.2 billion from 2023 to 2026 to support the deployment of climate-friendly vehicles, including fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs). The program covers the procurement of light and heavy commercial vehicles (EU classes N1, N2, and N3) and the development of hydrogen refueling stations (HRS). Incentives include up to 80% of the additional investment costs for alternative drive vehicles, up to 80% of eligible costs for HRS, and up to 50% for feasibility studies. Funding for heavy-duty vehicles is capped at €500,000 per application, and infrastructure funding requires at least one associated vehicle purchase under the program.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Tax Credit for Energy and Ecological Transition - Bonification d'impôts transition énergétique et écologique
description: The tax relief for investment in an ecological and energy transition project in Luxembourg includes incentives for businesses investing in renewable hydrogen. Eligible businesses can receive an 18% tax relief on investments and operating expenses related to producing or storing renewable hydrogen, which must meet the energy needs of the business by self-sufficient means. The goals of this initiative are to significantly decarbonize production processes, improve energy efficiency, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40%, contributing to a sustainable and environmentally friendly energy transition.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Tax incentives for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Tax incentives for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Funding Competition for Energy and Resource Efficiency - Förderwettbewerb Energie - und Ressourceneffizienz
description: This funding program, while not exclusively focused on Power-to-X (PtX), includes hydrogen as an eligible technology under its broader decarbonization scope. Across five rounds, total CAPEX funding increased from €15 million in the first two rounds to €40 million in the third and fourth, and €60 million in the fifth round in March 2025. Despite this, no funding has yet been allocated to hydrogen projects. Incentives include grants covering up to 60% of eligible costs, with a maximum of €20 million per project, and up to 5% of the net investment volume (capped at €50,000) for developing a savings concept.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Loan and loan guarantees for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Loan and loan guarantees for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Modernisation Grant (Nachhaltige Modernisierung von Binnenschiffe)
description: Program supports the decarbonization of inland vessels including dual-fuel engines and low-emission propulsion systems. Incentive: For emission-free vehicles: up to 100% of eligible costs for new builds, up to 80% for retrofitting. The first round was launched in July 2021 and the sixth round in November 2023. From 2024, the funding programme for the sustainable modernization of inland vessels will consist of three funding guidelines due to current developments in EU state aid law, namely the “Directive on the promotion of the sustainable modernization of inland vessels for the transfer of freight transport from road to waterway”, the “Directive on the promotion of emission-free and low-emission propulsion systems and the sustainable modernization of inland vessels” and the “Directive on the promotion of retrofitting of emission reduction equipment on inland vessels”. On January 1, 2027, the three funding guidelines are to be merged back into one. Within the second funding guideline a first call has been launched in March 2024
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: German Important Project of Common Interest (IPCEI) H2 projects
description: IPCEI Hydrogen aims to support the hydrogen ramp-up in Germany and Europe by promoting projects along the entire hydrogen value chain. IPCEI Hydrogen consists of several waves: Hy2Tech, Hy2Use, Hy2Infra, Hy2Move. 70% of the German projects in the IPCEI Hydrogen are co-financed by the federal government (BMWK, BMDV) and 30% by the federal states concerned. The total funding amount is around 13.5 billion euros. The specific funding amount for the respective hydrogen projects is approved by the European Commission on the basis of the funding gap. The Commission has already approved the four IPCEI waves Hy2Tech, Hy2Use, Hy2Infra and Hy2Move as well as several individual KUEBLL projects transferred from the IPCEI Hydrogen
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Funding Guidelines for International Hydrogen Projects - Förderrichtlinie für internationale Wasserstoffprojekte
description: Germany’s funding guidelines support international hydrogen pilot projects outside the EU and EFTA, aiming to test the integration of various technologies at specific sites and promote the industrial scaling of solutions previously demonstrated only at small scale. The program also includes hydrogen import projects and is structured into two modules: one for industrial application and experimental development, and another for basic and industrial research, scientific studies, and training. The first funding round took place in October 2021, followed by a second round in November 2024.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Lorry CO2-tolls (Federal Highways Toll Act)
description: Until the end of 2025, electric vehicles, hydrogen combustion engines and hydrogen fuel cell trucks are exempt from the CO2 toll. After that, these lorries will be charged 25% of the toll rate for infrastructure costs. This measure is the result of the revision of the Federal Highways Toll Act, which was changed in accordance with the change to the Eurovignette Directive that entered into effect in March 2022
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Carbon pricing instruments","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Carbon2Chem
description: Program volume of EUR 177 million for the first funding phase (2016-2020) and further EUR 84 million for the second phase (2020-2024). The general aim of the cluster project is to process steel mill gases for CCU to produce fuels, plastics or fertilizers. Each sub-project focusses on a part of the value chain, i.e. separation of exhaust gas or synthesis of a specific CCU product. Target is to use 20 Mtpa of CO2 from the steel production. Funding includes R&D, demonstration as well as CAPEX and OPEX for some facilities. Large parts of the project funding are dedicated to hydrogen (production, storage), and hydrogen derivatives (synthesis and use in different applications including personal transport), because hydrogen is the key chemical to re-use exhaust gas
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Grant "Hydrogen Republic of Germany" - Flagship Projects and Basic Research
description: The Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) has launched a research initiative with a budget exceeding €700 million to advance key hydrogen technologies. It focuses on three flagship projects: H2Giga, which supports the mass production of large-scale electrolysers; H2Mare, which explores hydrogen production at sea; and TransHyDE, which investigates hydrogen storage and transport solutions. The TransHyDE project alone received €145 million in funding for the 2021–2025 period.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Mission Hydrogen - Grant "8. Energieforschungsprogramms der BR"
description: Grant "8. Energieforschungsprogramms der BR", further projects with unlimited calls and unspecified volume are part of the programme. Funding programme for project-related R&D activities and the demonstration of innovative technical solutions.  Both hydrogen and hydrogen derivatives are eligible for funding. It contains a specific hydrogen mission.: under Mission Hydrogen, it states there is a target to reduce investment costs for electrolyzers  to below EUR 400/kW by 2030
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Grant: HC-H2 (Helmholtz Cluster Wasserstoff)
description: EUR 860 million until 2038 by the BMBF for R&D activities in the Rheinish mining area to transform it into a hydrogen model area
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Low Emissions Transport Fund
description: The Low Emissions Transport Fund (LETF) in New Zealand supports the adoption of low-emission fuels, including hydrogen, to decarbonize the transport sector. The fund aims to create an enabling regulatory environment, reduce barriers for consenting hydrogen projects, promote a cost-effective transition to a low-emissions economy, and support access to international investment and markets
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen certification
description: The voluntary “hydrogen” certification, focuses on products for constructing gas networks and installations under the H2INiG label. This certification, based on the PCW-17 program, aims to ensure compliance with specific assessment criteria, promoting safety, quality, and reliability in hydrogen-related infrastructure. The primary goals are to enhance the credibility of hydrogen technologies, support the development of a sustainable hydrogen economy, and encourage innovation in the sector.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Regulations","name":"Certification scheme thresholds","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Legislation – Constitution for hydrogen
description: The draft amendment to the Energy Law focuses on supporting hydrogen production and storage projects, facilitating the development of hydrogen infrastructure, and establishing a regulatory framework for hydrogen-related activities. The goals include promoting hydrogen as a key energy source, ensuring the development of necessary infrastructure, and providing revenue support mechanisms to encourage hydrogen production.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Amendment to the Act on electromobility and other alternative fuels in transport
description: The act focuses on promoting hydrogen as an alternative fuel by establishing a regulatory framework to support its production, distribution, and use in transportation and other sectors. The act aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy security, and foster innovation in clean energy technologies. Key goals include developing hydrogen infrastructure, incentivizing hydrogen-powered vehicles, and integrating hydrogen solutions into the national energy strategy.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title:
Regulation of the Minister for Climate and the Environment on the granting of aid
public for the development of hydrogen technologies and co-associating infrastructure 
under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan
description: The Polish regulation aims to support the development of hydrogen technologies and infrastructure as part of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Its goals include funding research, development, and deployment of hydrogen infrastructure to promote hydrogen as a clean energy source, contributing to Poland’s climate goals and energy transition.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Wodoryzacja Gospodarki  (Hydrogenisation of the Economy)
description: EUR 110 mln. The “Hydrogenization of the Economy” aims to develop a low- and zero-emission economy by supporting projects related to hydrogen-powered transport units. The program focuses on research, development, and commercialization of innovative hydrogen technologies, contributing to the economic potential of Poland. It aligns with the National Recovery and Resilience Plan and the Polish hydrogen strategy until 2030, with an outlook to 2040. The goal is to foster industry growth and achieve significant environmental and economic benefits.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Support for recharging infrastructure for electric vehicles and hydrogen refuelling infrastructure
description: PLN 100 mln. The Polish government program aims to support the development of hydrogen refueling infrastructure to reduce CO2 and NOx emissions and improve air quality. The program provides funding for the construction and modernization of public hydrogen refueling stations, ensuring they use low-emission hydrogen. The goal is to facilitate the transition to cleaner transportation by increasing the availability of hydrogen refueling points
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: New Energy Technologies
description:
PLN 800 million program led by Poland’s National Centre for Research and Development to support climate neutrality and energy security.
While not limited to hydrogen, it emphasizes hydrogen technologies for production and use, alongside goals like smart grid development, increased renewable energy share, emission reductions, and promotion of biodegradable raw materials.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Alternative Fuel Standards
description: Singapore plans to develop standards by 2025 for ammonia and methanol bunkering and for hydrogen refuelling  to support the trial of hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles. These are part of over 25 sustainability-related standards and accreditation programs aimed at enhancing greenhouse gas reporting, decarbonization, and renewable energy. EnterpriseSG, the national standards and accreditation body, will lead the effort together with two industry-led entities (Singapore Standards Council and Singapore Accreditation Council).
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Regulations","name":"Technical standards","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Maritime Singapore Green Initiative (MSGI)
description: The Maritime Singapore Green Initiative (MSGI) aims to reduce the environmental impact of shipping by promoting clean and green practices, including the adoption of hydrogen as a zero-emission fuel. The initiative includes incentives for ships using hydrogen fuel cells and other zero-emission technologies, with goals to encourage early adoption of these technologies and support Singapore’s transition to net-zero emissions
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Climate and innovation act, art.6
description: Article 6 of the Climate and Innovation Act (KIG) focuses on promoting innovative technologies, including hydrogen production and storage. The Act provides financial support to companies for implementing novel technologies and processes until 2030. The goal is to develop the domestic hydrogen market and infrastructure, contributing to Switzerland’s climate targets by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing energy security
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Exemption of the lump-sum heavy vehicle charge (PSVA) for Swiss vehicles
description: The Swiss Federal Office for Customs and Border Security states that zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs), including hydrogen-powered vehicles, are exempt from the performance-related and lump-sum heavy vehicle charges (LSVA and PSVA). This exemption aims to promote the use of cleaner transport options and reduce emissions by providing financial incentives for adopting ZEVs.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Tax incentives for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Tax incentives for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Innosuisse
description: The Innosuisse program, supported by the Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE), includes pilot projects that focus on innovative energy solutions, such as hydrogen technology. These projects aim to demonstrate the feasibility and potential of hydrogen as a sustainable energy source, aligning with Switzerland’s goals for energy transition and climate protection. The program supports the development and implementation of hydrogen initiatives to bridge the gap between research and market application.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Fuel cell research in Switzerland
description: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy’s fuel cell program focuses on hydrogen as a key element, supporting research and development to enhance fuel cell technology. The program aims to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and extend the service life of fuel cells, facilitating their use in various applications such as vehicles, stationary energy supply, and portable devices. By fostering collaboration among research institutions and private companies, the program seeks to advance prototypes and bring innovative hydrogen-based solutions to market
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen blending in distribution networks (2023)
description: The UK government has made a strategic policy decision to support blending up to 20% hydrogen by volume into Great Britain’s gas distribution networks. This initiative seeks to realise the potential strategic and economic benefits of hydrogen blending, with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) assessing its safety and feasibility on the basis of evidence from industry trials. The ultimate goal is to assess whether hydrogen blending can be safely and economically implemented, contributing to the UK’s low-carbon energy transition
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Tees Valley Hydrogen Transport Hub
description: £20 million. The Tees Valley Hydrogen Hub aimes exploring hydrogen’s potential in creating a cleaner and more efficient transport sector. The competition, run by Innovate UK, will see businesses and research groups collaborate to develop hydrogen as a reliable fuel source, addressing challenges like large-scale refueling and hydrogen use in public transport and heavy goods vehicles. The goals include reducing carbon emissions, improving air quality, fostering energy security, and creating hundreds of skilled jobs
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for demonstration projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Zero Emission Road Freight Demonstrator (ZERFD) Programme
description: The UK government has announced an investment (GBP 200 million) to launch the world’s largest fleet of zero-emission heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), including hydrogen fuel cell technology, as part of a three-year program to decarbonize road freight. The goals are to improve air quality, create greener jobs, reduce reliance on foreign oil, and ensure all new HGVs sold in the UK are zero-emission by 2040, supporting the UK’s COP26 pledges
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for demonstration projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: EPSRC hubs for lower TRL research, HyRES and HI-Act
description: £20million. The UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) has allocated £10 million to the UK-HyRES hub and £10 million to the HI-ACT hub as part of a larger £53 million investment to drive innovation towards a net zero energy sector by 2050. These hubs will focus on integrating clean and sustainable hydrogen into various energy systems, aiming to boost knowledge, create innovative green technologies, and reduce energy demand.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Energy Sector Fund
description: The Energy Sector Fund focuses on advancing green hydrogen technology in Uruguay. It aims to support research and development projects that innovate in the production, storage, and use of green hydrogen and derivatives, thereby promoting sustainability and reducing carbon emissions. The initiative encourages collaboration between academic institutions, research centers, and private companies, aiming to build technical capacity and stimulate economic growth through new markets and job opportunities. Projects are evaluated by a dedicated committee and can receive funding for up to 12 months
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Climate Protection Contracts
description: Germany has allocated €2.8 billion to support climate protection contracts, including but not limited to hydrogen-based technologies. Through the Carbon Contracts for Difference (CCfD) scheme, the program provides significant funding to help industries transition to low-carbon processes, such as green steel production using renewable hydrogen. The initiative supports compliance with the EU hydrogen taxonomy, which requires hydrogen to achieve at least a 70% reduction in lifetime greenhouse gas emissions compared to fossil fuel alternatives, and contributes to Germany’s broader goal of achieving climate neutrality by 2045.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Centralized purchase of hydrogen and biomethane program
description: €140 million. Portugal's centralized purchase program for hydrogen and biomethane, announced by the Minister for the Environment and Energy, involves an electronic auction managed by the Wholesale Supplier of Last Resort (CURg). The auction aims to purchase 150 GWh/year of biomethane at €62/MWh and 120 GWh/year of hydrogen at €127/MWh, The program's goals are to boost renewable gas production, integrate these gases into the National Gas System, and support the country's decarbonization efforts towards a zero net emissions economy.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Industrial Decarbonisation and Hydrogen Revenue Support (IDHRS)
description: The IDHRS scheme aims to provide long-term revenue support for hydrogen production and industrial carbon capture projects, facilitating final investment decisions and contributing to the UK's net zero emissions target by 2050. The scheme, backed by the Energy Bill, integrates with other funds like the Net Zero Hydrogen Fund (NZHF) and the CCUS Infrastructure Fund (CIF) to support the development of low-carbon hydrogen technologies and industrial decarbonisation
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Priority Research Programme and Equipment on Decarbonised Hydrogen - PERP-H2
description: €83 million (not jusst for hydrogen). The PEPR-H2 program, part of France's national strategy for decarbonized hydrogen, aims to advance R&D in hydrogen production, storage, and transport, with a focus on low to intermediate technology readiness levels (TRL 1-4). It supports innovative projects like high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen use in heavy mobility, and advanced storage solutions. The program's goals include developing next-generation materials and systems, fostering industrial breakthroughs, and ensuring the safe, efficient deployment of hydrogen technologies.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: 15-year CfD scheme to close cost gap
description:
A 15-year CfD scheme supports domestic and imported hydrogen, requiring at least 10 years of operation post-subsidy. Amendments to the JOGMEC Act (effective 2025) enable support for both supply and demand, including hub development.

Eligibility requires supply to hard-to-abate sectors (e.g. industry, transport); power sector-only proposals are ineligible. Projects must start before 2030.

Application window: Nov 22 – Mar 31, 2025
Evaluation: Begins Jan 31, 2025
Reference price: Based on conventional or fossil hydrogen prices
Minimum size: 1 ktpa
May 2025: 27 bids received; results to be announced through April 2026
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Contracts for difference","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hub Support Scheme (project development support)
description:
JPY 5.7 billion (USD 38 million) for the FY2025-2026 (to be approved). Subsidies under the Hub Support Scheme will be awarded to developers of domestic transport and storage facilities needed for the use of low-carbon hydrogen and its derivatives, for a portion of the costs for Front-End Engineering Design (FEED), engineering, and construction. Grants to be used my more than two companies. The application process for the subsidies under the Hub Support Scheme will likely be similar to the process for the CfD Scheme
The first batch of applications will be evaluated after June 30, 2025
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Modernization Fund for public transport
description: CZK 7.3 billion (USD 320 million) for the purchase of new electric of hydrogen-powered buses, trolleybuses or trams. Up to 50% of the eligible costs (difference with an ICE) can be funded. Applications will be open from March 2025 to January 2026. Projects must be implemented within 42 months from receiving the funds. Maximum incentives for hydrogen are USD 44k for buses (trams do not have a fuel, but it is assumed that those are electric)
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Catalogue of industries encouraged for foreign investment
description: This is a list of sectors where foreign investment is encouraged for equipment manufacturing. Production of renewable hydrogen is included, as well as storage, transportation, liquefaction, hydrogen fuel cells, and HRS. There were previous versions of the list in 2019 and 2020
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Funding regime for off-grid renewable hydrogen production
description: Focused on innovation for low-carbon hydrogen production from fossil fuels and renewable electricity as well as hydrogen storage in porous reservoirs. It aims to work on new principles and technologies for hydrogen production, improving efficiency (including electricity transmission and conversion to hydrogen using DC off-grid hydrogen production), identify the transport mechanisms for hydrogen in porous reservoirs
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Green and Low Carbon Transition Industry Guidance
description: Projects for renewable hydrogen production or for the manufacturing of relevant equipment would be eligible for support via preferential loans, subsidies, and simplified administrative procedures. Guidance does not provide details
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - Transposition of the industry target
description: The National Energy and Climate Plan estimates that 270 ktpa of RFNBO will be needed in 2030 to satisfy the industry target. The private sector (Orlen) estimates 212 ktpa for industry (254 ktpa in total for RED)
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition for industry and transport
description: The government held a public consultation on the Renewable Energy Directive transposition from July to September 2024, with final legislation still pending. As of July 2025, a new consultation is underway on transport quotas. The proposal includes a 2.5% RFNBO quota for transport by 2030, with no general transport quotas before then. However, there are phased quotas for hydrogen use in refineries, starting at 0.25% in 2027 and rising to 1.5% by 2030. Multipliers apply 2x for general transport and 1.5x for aviation and shipping. The proposal includes no penalties for non-compliance.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Subsidy for hydrogen hubs
description: EUR 100-125 million for local hydrogen hubs using electrolyser of 2.5-25 MW along with storage and transport infrastructure and end-use applications. Several companies can apply together, but the facilities should be within 5 km. Scope: CAPEX for all parts of the value chain and OPEX for production and use. Hubs focusing on the transport sector or linked to the planned hydrogen backbone are excluded
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Hubs","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Incentive Programme 3: (grandes demostradores de electrólisis y proyectos innovadores de producción de hidrógeno renovable Programa de incentivos 3)
description: EUR 100 mln. The "Programa de incentivos 3" aims to support large-scale electrolyzer demonstrators and innovative renewable hydrogen production projects. The program's goals include developing and integrating electrolyzers with a capacity above 20 MW in industrial contexts, ensuring the use of 100% renewable electricity, and advancing hydrogen production technology.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Environmental and climate protection support scheme
description: The scheme aims for carbon neutrality by 2050, with a 55% emission reduction by 2030. It offers subsidies for hydrogen vehicles, industrial equipment, production facilities, and networks to support a hydrogen economy and reduce emissions. CAPEX subsidies to acquire hydrogen vehicles (clean vehicles), hydrogen consuming equipment in industries (decarbonising processes), to set up hydrogen production capcity, and to build hydrogen networks
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"},{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: EUR 960 million to support investment in strategic sectors
description: EUR 960 million for investment in strategic sectors (batteries, solar panels, wind turbines, heat-pumps, electrolysers and carbon capture usage and storage). Funding will be allocated as direct grants. Funding under the Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework (TCTF). Funds to be granted before the end of 2025

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition of the transport target
description:
Public consultation held ahead of the 21 May deadline for transposing EU targets into national legislation.
Denmark finalized legislation in May 2025, setting a GHG reduction target and a combined biofuels and RFNBO quota of 5.1% by 2030, with a minimum of 0.9% RFNBO. Aviation fuels count toward the target but are exempt from the obligation. Due to multipliers for RFNBO and renewable electricity, the effective RFNBO target is lower than the nominal 1%. Projects receiving public support are proposed to be excluded from target compliance.

title: FEED support for domestic production of e-SAF
description:
EUR 200 million of total budget (under France 2030) with the first four projects receiving EUR 100 million. Covers up to 60-80% (depending on the type of company) FEED costs for e-SAF projects. Open from Dec 23 to Jun 24
In April 2025, Four projects with a total estimated production of 270 ktpa of e-SAF were selected (national goal of 500 ktpa of SAF by 2030)
Kereauzen, 70 ktpa, COD 2031, hydrogen from a 275 MW electrolyzer, CO2 from bioethanol
Take kair, 37.5 ktpa, COD 2030, hydrogen from a 200 MW electrolyzer, CO2 from cement

title: Subsidies for FCEV program (Round 3)
description: China has allocated CNY 2.34 billion (USD 330 million) in its latest round of funding to support fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV) development, bringing the total FCEV program funding to CNY 5.11 billion (USD 700 million) over the past few years. This funding targets seven provinces and three cities, with the top three recipients being Hebei (CNY 793 million), Beijing (CNY 450 million), and Henan (CNY 420 million), reflecting a strong regional push to scale up hydrogen mobility infrastructure and adoption.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

description: CNY 1.14 billion (USD 157 million) for provinces and cities in 2023

title: Incentives under the Investment Law - Cabinet Decree 20 from 2022
description: The Investment Law provides the legal framework for both local and foreign investment in Egypt. Article 20 defines that companies and projects in strategic sectors can receive a single license for the estabilshment, operation and management of the project. The Cabinet Decree 20 from 2022 explicitly identifies production, storage and export of renewable hydrogen and ammonia as areas of strategic importance (benefiting from Article 20) Article 11 of the Investment Law defines two geographical zones where projects can be receive 30-50% deduction of their taxable income and up to 80% of the paid-up capital at the time of commencement of the project (called Special Incentive). Cabinet Decree 981 from 2022 recognizes production, storage and export of renewable hydrogen and ammonia as industrial sectors that can benefit from the Special Incentive
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Tax incentives for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Incentives under the Investment Law - Cabinet Decree 981 from 2022
description: Article 11 of the Investment Law defines two geographical zones where projects can be receive 30-50% deduction of their taxable income and up to 80% of the paid-up capital at the time of commencement of the project (called Special Incentive). Cabinet Decree 981 from 2022 recognizes production, storage and export of renewable hydrogen and ammonia as industrial sectors that can benefit from the Special Incentive. There are also several additional incentives that can be granted by a Cabinet decision

title: Incentives under the Investment Law - Cabinet Decree 20 from 2022
description: The General Authority for Free Zones and Investment (GAFI) must coordinate with all the relevant ministries to select the priority projects that would be eligible for additional incentives from Article 13 of the Investment Law and the type of incentives that would be offered. When identifying the priority projects, ministries and governmental entities must take into account that they would contribute to the state’s economic development strategy, which expressly includes green economy projects

title: Land use agreement
description: Thirteen companies are assessing the production of renewable hydrogen in Jordan. Two (Amarenco and FFI) completed a preliminary study and have signed a land agreement with the government. They will proceed to perform an economic feasibility study in the selected lands. Seven other companies have completed their preliminary study and are currently in the process of negotiating the land agreement. The remaining four are in the conducting the preliminary study
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen Power Generation Bidding Market - Clean - Round 2
description: In 2025, a second hydrogen auction will award 3 TWh of low-carbon hydrogen and 1.3 TWh of hydrogen-based power (no GHG criteria) under 15-year contracts starting in 2028. The auction is open to imports and various technologies, with bid price (60%) as the main evaluation factor, alongside certification (14%), local content (6%), and emissions reduction (4%). Applications close between July and September 2025, with results expected by November. Key changes include FX indexation and flexible volume adjustments. Around 15 projects are expected to be supported.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Market access for the hydrogen networks
description: In November 2024, ACM published new rules for third-party access (TPA) to hydrogen terminals. The Netherlands will use negotiated TPA which means the terminal operator and potential user of the terminal will make agreements on the conditions and rates for terminal use. The rules entered into force from February 2025
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Market access","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Gas Supply Act amendment
description: The amendment extends the Gas Supply Act (gasforsyningsloven) to hydrogen since 1 January 2023. The Act provides the legal framework for the establishment, ownership, operation, and regulation of hydrogen transport and storage systems. It covers technical requirements, third-party access, tariff methodologies, and system responsibility, and authorizes the Minister for Energy to set detailed rules as needed. As a follow-up the government will present a proposal for political review concerning ownership, operation and financing of the hydrogen infrastructure
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Market access","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Political agreements for hydrogen infrastructure regulation
description:
First political agreement on hydrogen infrastructure reached in March 2023, establishing Energinet as the developer/operator of the transmission network and Evida for the distribution network.
A second agreement in April 2024 defined the economic framework and risk-sharing model for the hydrogen backbone from Esbjerg to Germany.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Market access","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen demand initiative
description:
The consortium is meant to support the H2hubs by designing and implementing demand-side support mechanisms in order to facilitate purchases of hydrogen produced by the H2Hubs, with the aim of helping to provide offtake certainty and unlock FID. The measures and implementation plan should be ready by the end of 2024. The consortium consists of consists of the EFI Foundation (EFIF), S&P Global (S&P) and the financial exchange operator Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). There are 8 partners in total
H2DI assessed 12 mechanisms and proposed two to the DoE. One of those was a joint offtake producter auction (JOPA) where the supply and demand submit a joint bid with the cost gap to be subsidized. The EVP of EFI foundation (part of the consortium) estimates that demand triggered will be enough for 20 fuel cell buses
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Hubs","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition of transport target
description: Public consultation for the transposition. The proposed regulation has GHG emissions reduction quotas that fuel suppliers would have to meet for 2026-2035 and it would replace the TIRUERT scheme. There are specific sub-quotas for low-carbon hydrogen and RFNBO (0.1% in 2026, 1.5% in 2030, 2% in 2035) without any multiplier. From 2030, the share of low-carbon hydrogen would be capped (to 0.8%) to meet the EU quotas for renewable hydrogen. The consultation document does not specify if hydrogen used in refineries would count towards the target. Quotas for specific sectors are also included (1.2% in 2030, 2% in 2032, 5% in 2035 for aviation and 1.2% in 2030 and 2% for 2034 for shipping). Proposed penalty for non-compliance is EUR 80/GJ (EUR 9.6/kg) for RFNBO, which would be on top of penalties for missing the GHG reduction targets (which have a penalty of EUR 700/tCO2)
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: 130 ktpa tender - State of Maharashtra
description: A total of 130 ktpa of renewable hydrogen capacity is being offered, anchored by a large project of 50–100 ktpa and supported by 2–15 smaller projects producing 2–15 tonnes per day each. All projects must be completed within 36 months and operate for at least 25 years. Incentives include a 30% CAPEX subsidy for the anchor project and 15% for smaller ones, along with full exemptions from electricity duty (15 years), stamp duty, and local land taxes, plus 50% off intra-state transmission and wheeling charges for 20 years. Subsidy stacking is allowed. Project evaluation will consider local manufacturing (minimum 55% of components) and the share of electricity generated within the state. The anchor project must sell at least 50% of its output domestically, while smaller projects must sell 100% domestically.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Liquid Hydrogen Carrier Demonstration Project
description: Document drafted by the government envisioning that the three largest shipbuilding companies will work towards the demonstration and commercialization of liquid hydrogen ships. The plan includes a total investment of KRW 55.5 billion in 2025. A demonstration vessel (2000 m3) is to be designed by 2025 with construction in 2026-2027 and verification in 2028. After testing in 2028, the technology is expected to be completed by 2030. Subsequent plans include developing a 40000 m3 carrier by 2032 and one 160000 m3 carrier by 2040
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Land allocation for hydrogen by 2030

policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Administrative measures","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen innovation and demonstration
description: Support innovation and demonstration work, enabling the development or improvement of components and systems linked to the production, transport of hydrogen and its uses. The call is split in two rounds in Sept 2025 and April 2026 and will remain open until September 2026. This is part of the annual hydrogen budget that ADEME has which was EUR 20 million in 2024. ADEME covers up to 50% of the costs and the minimum share of private investment is EUR 300k. The research grant is meant to cover all the equipment necessary for the research excluding items like certification and standardization of the equipment among others. There are also caps to the share of management costs (7% of eligible costs) and salaries
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Australia has allocated AUD 8 billion for renewable hydrogen production
description: The AUD 8 billion for production support will cover: the Hydrogen Production Tax Incentive (AUD 6.7 billion over 10 years); additional funding for the Hydrogen Headstart program (AUD 1.3 billion over 10 years); funds to deliver the 2024 National Hydrogen Strategy (AUD 17 million over four years). Furthermore, renewable hydrogen will be supported through the Future Made in Australia Innovation fund which supports innovation, commercialization, pilot and demonstration projects, and early state development (AUD 1.7 billion over 10 years). AUD 11.4 million over four years will be used to fast track "the initial phase of the Guarantee of Origin Scheme for green hydrogen and bring forward work on green metals, including iron, steel and aluminum." AUD 10 million will be given in 2025–26 to establish a National Hydrogen Technology Skills Training Center to promote hydrogen workforce development.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Tax incentives for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Hydrogen-to-power (H2P) consultation response.
description: The UK government has committed to introduce a business model to support hydrogen-powered electricity generation, with a market engagement document promised in spring 2025. The Hydrogen to Power Business Model will be based on a dispatchable power agreement-style mechanism to support the deployment of hydrogen-to-power technology. Developing dispatchable hydrogen-powered generation is part of the government’s Clean Power Mission and contributes to the country’s efforts to reach net-zero GHG emissions by 2050. The National Energy System Operator estimates that Great Britain's electricity system could need  about 40-45 GW of long-duration flexible capacity by 2030.

title: Subsidies for fuel cell commercial vehicles
description: The government will provide subsidies of JPY 700/kg (USD 4.8/kg) to promote the use of FCEV for commercial transport such as truck and buses in five regions of the country (Tokyo, Fukushima, Kanagawa, Aichi, Hyogo). Subsidy is roughly equivalent to three quarters of the cost difference between hydrogen and diesel. The government will encourage local governments to also take their own support measures, thereby significantly reducing the burden on private operators. Through the scheme, METI aims to have FCEV represent at least 3% of the total number of general purpose vehicles and passenger cars in the prefecture, of which large trucks must account for 10pc or more by 2030
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Grants for demand","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition of transport target
description: Plans to expand the Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation currently covering biofuels in road transport. Combined biofuels and RFNBO targets are 8% in 2026 increasing to 11%, 14%, 18%, 21.5% towards 2030. The RFNBO targets start at 0.1% in 2028 to 1% in 2029 and 2.5% in 2030. The proposed 2.5% target is higher than the 1% in RED to make sure Ireland meets the RED target despite the use of bonus credits by fuel suppliers which could count hydrogen more than once. This is the same reason why the combined quota (21.5%) is also above the RED quota (5.5%). In the current RTFO, RFNBO can generate certificates that are 4x the energy content of the fuels
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition of transport target
description: RFNBO quotas are expected to be introduced by a draft act amending the biocomponents and liquid biofuels act and the renewable energy sources act. Changes are expected to be enacted by Q2 2026

title: DM Opex - CfD for industry and transport
description: The 2024 National Climate and Energy Plans (NCEP) propose a measure to stimulate investment in hard-to-abate sectors by introducing a legislative framework with four key objectives: defining renewable hydrogen, establishing specific operational expenditure (OPEX) incentives, setting eligibility criteria for accessing these incentives, and outlining rules for combining them with other funding sources. The incentive is expected to take the form of a Contract for Difference (CfD), disbursed monthly over a 10-year period. This measure aims to support the production of up to 250,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually by 2027.

title: Regulation of the hydrogen network and market
description: Proposal legislation open for public consultation until mid June 2025. Three main aspects are covered: Hydrogen network regulation; Certification; and Incentives. For the hydrogen network, it covers the transposition of the EU Directive 2024/1788 on common rules for internal markets focusing on limited hydrogen networks (Articles 43-46). For certification, it defines the governance system including certificate system, administrative details and monitoring. Specific incentives are not defined but page 29 indicates that hydrogen projects can be eligible to various incentives including up to 100% support within designated zones, support framework for infrastructure and potentially operational aid
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for R&D projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

description: Businesses may receive a tax credit for the purchase of hydrogen or natural gas from a Regional Clean Hydrogen Hub in Pennsylvania. title: Tax credit for hydrogen use (Illinois)

policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Incentives and investments","name":"Tax incentives","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Grant for electric buses

title: Hydrogen safety regulations
description: The Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment (MBIE) and WorkSafe will review and update key electricity and gas safety regulations to enable safe production, storage, and use of hydrogen in near-term uses. Doing this involves a mix of changes to regulations and streamlining how standards relating to hydrogen are updated in legislation. The Government is moving to streamline how standards are updated in regulation. The Government will consult in mid 2025 on proposals for hydrogen health and safety regulatory settings
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Regulations","name":"Technical standards","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Tax incentives
description: A bill was introduced in the Senate for a regulatory framework for hydrogen. Incentives include tax credits and exemptions on custom duties on imported goods. Scope includes hydrogen production, distribution and storage. The private sector advocates for the programs to be active for 20 years for renewable hydrogen and 10 years for production from fossil fuels with CCUS with the incentives granted for 30 and 15 years respectively
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Tax incentives for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Grants for HRS
description: The grant program supports companies investing in electric and hydrogen recharging/refueling infrastructure, aiming for climate neutrality by 2050 and a 55% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Subsidies will be awarded through competitive calls for projects, with a maximum budget of EUR 7 million per call. This ensures transparency and promotes innovative, high-quality infrastructure development. Subsidies for electric and hydrogen recharging/refuelling infrastructure. Call for projects will be organized once entered into force
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Infrastructure","name":"Grants for infrastructure","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Pilot demonstration program
description: China’s National Energy Administration published a plan for pilot initiatives across 11 areas of the hydrogen value chain targeting commercial deployment by June 2028. Each project should demonstrate technological progression, commercial potential, substantial carbon reduction benefits, and replicable frameworks. For hydrogen production, electrolyzers should be of at least 100 MW predominantly powered by paired renewable energy, with no more than 20% of renewable power fed into the grid. Minimum length for hydrogen pipelines is 100 km and minimum size for storage projects is 20000 Nm3. NEA focuses on uses for refining, coal-to-liquid replacement, power generation and long duration energy storage with at least 1000 tpa of use
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for demonstration projects","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage Cluster Sequencing Process - Track 2
description:
UK has the target of selecting 4 CCUS clusters for development by 2030. In July 2023, two clusters were selected under Track-2: Acorn (North East) and Viking (Humber). Phase-1 was the selection of the clusters, while Phase-2 was the application of specific projects within those clusters. Combined storage capacity of 18 Mtpa
Acorn captures industrial CO2 emissions from assets around the St Fergus Terminal, expected to use 175 miles of repurposed pipelines and store at least 5 Mtpa. Viking will capture CO2 from industrial assets in the Humber region and plans to capture 10 Mtpa by 2030 and 15 Mtpa by 2035. FID for Viking is planned for 2025
In June 2025 development funding of GBP 200 million provided to both projects subject to business case. As the project develops, funding will also provide financial cover for the National Gas SCO₂T Connect project
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Resource push","name":"Grants for supply","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Renewable Energy Directive - National transposition for transport
description: A draft bill under consultation as part of the 2024 revision of Germany’s GHG reduction framework introduces binding RFNBO (Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin) quotas for fuel suppliers, starting at 0.1% in 2026 and rising to 1.5% by 2030 and 12% by 2040. The bill also extends GHG quota compliance to the aviation sector and sets non-compliance penalties at €17,000 per tonne for aviation and €8.4 per kilogram for other sectors. While the existing GHG quota system supports RFNBOs with multipliers, this new measure complements it by mandating specific volume offtake. The draft includes a multiplier of 1.5 for aviation and shipping, but none for road transport, and is expected to come into force by January 2026.
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Blending obligation for power plants
description: As part of the Multi-Year Program 2026, measures were introduced to achieve a full decarbonization of the power sector by 2035. This included a blending obligation for CO2-free energy carriers in gas-fired power stations of 1% by 2030 and 5% from 2032. System will be based on credit trading, so not all the gas plants need to be blend the minimum quota
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Market pull","name":"Mandates and quota","category":"Hydrogen"}]

title: Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF)
description: The updated State aid framework simplifies rules across five key areas to accelerate the energy transition:  deployment of renewables and low-carbon fuels, temporary electricity price relief for energy-intensive industries, decarbonization of existing industrial facilities,  development of clean tech manufacturing, and  de-risking clean energy investments. Key changes include raising the subsidy cap to 100% of eligible costs for RFNBO (renewable fuels of non-biological origin) production through competitive bidding, and up to 60% for industrial hydrogen use when at least 40% of the electricity mix is renewable. The framework also introduces accelerated depreciation and more flexible cumulation rules, allowing projects to combine funding from multiple sources such as IPCEI, CEF, and the Innovation Fund.

title: Clean and Low-Carbon Hydrogen Energy Evaluation Standards
description: Uruguay’s Green Hydrogen Sector Fund, established by ANII, MIEM, and LATU, aims to finance research, innovation, and training projects related to the construction, production, and use of green hydrogen and its derivatives in sectors such as transport, fertilizers, synfuels, and blending. Projects must involve electrolyzers with a minimum capacity of 1.5 MW, and applicants can include national legal entities or consortia with proven experience operating electrolyzers of at least 1 MW. The fund offers up to USD 10 million in non-reimbursable financing, with disbursement over a maximum of 10 years from the plant’s operational start. Priority is given to projects with early commissioning, with a final deadline of December 2025. However, as of 2025, the selected winner did not receive funding, and it remains undecided how the funds will be reallocated
policyType: [{"topic":"Fuels","family":"Regulations","name":"Certification scheme methodology","category":"Hydrogen"}]

- Mission Mode Projects (0-5 years): Focus on product development, e.g., modular electrolysers and PEM fuel cells.
- Grand Challenge Projects (0-8 years): Consortium mode projects targeting critical technology components like membrane electrode assemblies, catalysts, gas diffusion layers, etc.

title: Resolution 58/2024
description:
Resolution 58/2024 establishes objectives and guidelines for the detection, control, monitoring, quantification, and reduction of methane emissions from hydrocarbon activities in the province of Chubut, with the aim of reducing their impact on the environment. The regulation covers exploration, exploitation, and transportation activities.

The regulation prohibits venting of natural gas from oil and gas well testing when it exceeds 30 days (Art. 6), except for ensuring operational safety (Art. 7).

In addition, the regulation requires operators to submit an annual Methane Emissions Management Plan to the implementing authority, including:
  • an asset inventory, including the identification and classification of sources or potential sources of emissions
  • annual quantification of methane emissions and justification of emission factors or measurement methodologies, and/or quantification used
  • a Natural Gas Flaring Program 
  • an annual Leak Detection and Repair Program
(Art. 9-12)

The annual Leak Detection and Repair Program must progressively cover all new and existing facilities, consider all potential sources of methane emissions, and at minimum contain the following:
  • Annual monitoring plan, including inspection frequency schedule and detection-oriented activities
  • Leak repair plan based on prioritisation criteria defined by the operator over a one-year period
  • If applicable, action plan for replacement of components and/or equipment based on the prioritisation 
  • Progress of the implementation of the Leak Detection and Repair Program
(Art. 13-14)

The regulation obligates operators to detect and identify methane leaks and any other sources of methane emissions (Art. 15). 

Non-compliance with the regulation may be sanctioned by means of a warning or fines (Art. 26).

title: MEMR Regulation No. 26 of 2018 on the Implementation of Good Mining Practices and Supervision of Mineral and Coal Mining
description:
Regulation of the Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources No. 26 of 2018 on the Implementation of Good Mining Practices and Supervision of Mineral and Coal Mining provides the regulatory framework for the implementation of good mining practices and the supervision of mineral and coal mining activities in Indonesia. It aims to ensure that mining operations are conducted responsibly, with attention to environmental management, reclamation, and post-mining obligations, while empowering inspectors to enforce compliance.

Good Mining Practices include:
  • Environmental management in accordance with the license holder’s Environmental Impact Analysis (AMDAL)
  • Prevention and restoration of the environment in the event of environmental pollution or damage.
  • Reclamation and post-mining obligations, such as the requirement for licence holders to submit and implement reclamation and post-mining plans, deposit guarantee funds and report the implementation of the plan to the relevant authority.
The regulation empowers mining inspectors to supervise mining activities by evaluating periodic reports submitted by licence holders, conducting periodic inspections, assessing the successful implementation of programmes and activities, suspend mining activities that pose environmental or safety risks and recommend permanent termination of operations if violations persist.

title: Mineral Output Statistical Evaluation System
description:
The Mineral Output Statistical Evaluation System (MOSES) is Zambia’s digital traceability platform designed to monitor and regulate the production and export of key minerals. Developed in 2016 by the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) in collaboration with UNCTAD, MOSES was introduced to combat illicit financial flows, improve transparency and ensure accurate revenue collection in the mining sector. It primarily applies to high-value and strategic minerals, including copper, gold, emeralds, amethyst, tin, and manganese. These minerals are tracked from the point of extraction to export, making MOSES a cornerstone of Zambia’s mineral governance framework.

Key Measures Under Zambia’s MOSES Traceability System include:
  • Electronic Export Permit System
    All mineral exports must be registered and approved through the MOSES platform. Exporters are required to submit documentation such as licences, tax clearance certificates and mineral evaluation reports.
  • Mandatory Monthly Reporting
    Mining companies must submit monthly production and export data electronically. This digital process replaces manual reporting, reducing delays and improving data accuracy.
  • Real-Time Monitoring
    MOSES tracks minerals such as copper from the point of extraction to export. It cross-verifies production data with export permits and customs declarations, monitoring transport routes, quantities and declared values to detect discrepancies or underreporting.
  • Integration with Other Government Systems
    MOSES is integrated with the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) and other regulatory bodies. This enables real-time data sharing and enforcement, ensuring taxes and royalties are correctly assessed and collected.
  • Automated Alerts and Analytics
    The system flags anomalies or suspicious patterns, such as sudden drops in reported production or exports to countries that do not report receiving Zambian minerals, for example Switzerland.
  • Minerals Covered by MOSES
    The system applies to high-value and strategic minerals including copper, gold, emeralds, amethyst, tin and manganese. Industrial minerals such as limestone and gypsum are excluded and handled manually.

title: Ministerial Regulation No. 6 of 2021 - Hazardous and Toxic Waste (B3) Management
description:
Regulation of the Minister of Environment and Forestry Number 6 of 2021 on Procedure and Requirements for the Management of Hazardous and Toxic Waste provides the technical procedures and requirements for the management of hazardous and toxic waste (B3) in Indonesia. It implements Government Regulation No. 22/2021 on environmental protection and replaces several earlier frameworks. The regulation applies to all sectors handling B3 waste, including mining, energy, and industrial operations and applies toall entities involved in the generation, collection, utilisation, processing, stockpiling and dumping of B3 waste, with a focus on environmental safety and regulatory compliance. 

Stockpiling
B3 waste originating from mineral ore smelting and mineral ore processing or refining may be stockpiled through replacement of such waste in the former-mining area, either in a surface mining shaft or underground mining shaft. 

B3 waste in the form of tailings can be stockpiled in mining waste storage dams. The implementation of mine waste stockpiling must meet the prescribed technical requirements, including the need for a waste disposal plan and a closure and post-closure plan for the stockpiling facility.

Dumping
Certain waste may be dumped into the sea, including: (a) tailings; (b) drilling dust from exploration or exploitation activity using synthetic-based mud; and (c) non-B3 waste in the form of drilling dust or drilling mud from exploration or exploitation activity using water-based mud. 

To conduct waste dumping, waste producers must obtain an approval from the central government and must meet: 
  • Waste treatment standards (neutralisation or toxicity reduction)
  • Location standards (baseline sea quality must meet water quality norms)
  • Dumping procedures
  • Environmental monitoring of sea water, sediments, and ecosystems
Monitoring
Producers, collectors, utilisers, processors and stockpilers of B3 waste are required to monitor B3 waste storage activities. Monitoring includes:
  • inspecting waste storage facilities such as, relocation in former mines, dams, injection wells etc.
  • supervising the collection of waste
  • recording the incoming and outgoing waste from a facility
  • routinely reporting data to the authorities (including about the type and amount of B3 waste produced, stored and submitted to collectors, utilisers and processors).
Utilisation
B3 waste may be recovered or recycled into usable products (e.g., raw materials, fuels). The following standards need to be met for waste utilisation:
  • submission of a utilisation plan to the Ministry of Environment; and
  • submission of technical approvals and a utilisation process that contains information about the amount of B3 waste utilised and the implementation period of waste utilisation activities
Licensing
Businesses that conduct B3 waste management must obtain technical approvals of two types:
  • Technical Approval (or PLB3 TA)
  • Certificate of Operational Feasibility (SLO-PLB3)
Waste collection, utilisation, processing and stockpiling require both PLB3 TA and SLO-PLB3, while waste dumping only needs PLB3 TA.

title: Decree 1827 K/30/MEM/2018 of 2018 - Guidelines for the Implementation of Good Mining Governance
description:
Ministerial Decree No. 1827 K/30/MEM/2018 issued by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources provides technical guidelines for the implementation of good mining governance in mineral and coal mining operations. It complements MEMR Regulation No. 26/2018 by detailing standard operating procedures (SOPs) for environmental management, safety, and operational oversight. The decree supports Indonesia’s broader goals of sustainable mining and environmental compliance.

Key provisions include:
  • Environmental Management:
    • Tailing dams must be designed, built, and operated safely, preventing pollution of surface and groundwater.
    • Tailing facilities must include emergency response systems and structural failure mitigation plans.
  • Mine Waste and Overburden Handling:
    • Prioritize refilling former mining pits to support mineral conservation.
    • If overburden is stockpiled outside the mining site, it must follow a safe distance assessment from residential areas, public facilities, water bodies, and agricultural land.
  • Technical Oversight:
    • Provides SOPs for the appointment and evaluation of key technical personnel
  • Safety and Compliance:
    • Includes guidelines for mining safety, processing safety, and compliance monitoring.
    • Supports integration of environmental and safety considerations into Work Plan and Budget (RKAB) submissions.

title: MoEF Regulation No. 5 of 2022 - Wastewater Processing for Mining Businesses and/or Activities by Using Constructed Wetland Methods
description:
Regulation No. 5 of 2022 on Wastewater Processing for Mining Businesses and/or Activities by Using Constructed Wetland Methods issued by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry of the Republic of Indonesia provides technical requirements and procedures for the processing of wastewater from mining activities using constructed wetland methods. It implements Government Regulation No. 22/2021 on environmental protection and applies to both primary and supporting wastewater sources in mining operations. The regulation aims to reduce pollutant loads before discharge into the environment and promote sustainable water management practices.

The regulation covers wastewater from nickel mining, copper mining, other mineral mining, including cobalt, lithium and rare earth elements. It covers both wastewater from primary processes (i.e. runoff water, wastewater from mining pits, and/or wastewater from processing and refinery) and wastewater from supporting processes (i.e. domestic wastewater in mining area, wastewater from workshop activities and wastewater from laboratories). It sets down technical requirements for the facilities for constructed wetland processing, including their location and design. It also requires monitoring and maintenance of the facilities.

Processed wastewater using the constructed wetlands method may be disposed into surface water bodies such as rivers, streams, lakes and swamps. The disposal must be closely monitored, evaluated, and reported. The person in charge of the mining activity must:
  • Monitor the quality of the wastewater, quality of the surface water body, and the operations of the processing facilities. 
  • Evaluate the result of the monitoring by comparing against the quality standards set in its Environmental Approval and the quality standards set by the government (for the disposal target)
  • Submit the result of the evaluation as a report to the relevant authorities.

title: MOE Regulation No. 09 of 2006 on Wastewater Quality Standards for Nickel Ore Mining
description:
Regulation of the State Minister of Environment Number 09 of 2006 on Wastewater Quality Standards for Nickel Ore Mining Businesses and/or Activities sets out guidelines concerning the wastewater quality standards for nickel ore mining businesses and activities, which are defined to include mining (extraction, transportation and stockpiling), processing (crushing, grinding, floatation, leaching, concentration, drying, smelting, and purification), and mine closure activities. 

It stipulates the maximum levels and numbers of pollutants that may be present in the wastewater that is discharged into water sources from nickel ore mining businesses and activities. However, a stricter standard would apply if the result of a business/activity’s feasibility study as part of its environmental license (AMDAL or UKL-UPL) requires a stricter wastewater quality standard than that stipulated in the regulation.

Wastewater originating from nickel ore mining is required to be processed such that it does not exceed the applicable wastewater quality standard. The person in charge of the nickel mining business/activity is required to:
  • conduct a study of the location of wastewater treatment points to obtain a wastewater discharge permit
  • conduct daily self-monitoring of wastewater quality 
  • periodically examine the processed wastewater for adherence to applicable standards in an accredited laboratory at least once a month
  • analyse the wastewater and submit reports of the result at least once every three months every year to the relevant authorities. 
These obligations are relevant considerations for the issuance of a wastewater discharge permit in accordance with the prevailing regulation.

title: MEMR Regulation No. 43/2018 - Divestment Procedures for Foreign Mining Companies in Indonesia
description:
MEMR Regulation No. 43 of 2018 updates and streamlines Indonesia’s approach to foreign share divestment in mineral and coal mining companies. It builds on the foundation laid by MEMR Regulation No. 9 of 2017, which established the original divestment schedule and valuation principles. Together, these regulations aim to increase domestic ownership in mining operations and ensure strategic control over natural resources.

The regulation applies to companies holding IUP and IUPK licenses (production operation mining business licenses or IUP and special mining business licenses IUPK) and requires 51% domestic ownership by year 10.

Key provisions under MEMR 43/2018: 
  • Allows divestment to be fulfilled through new share issuance, not just transfer of existing shares.
  • Simplifies the process by removing the requirement for a tender mechanism, enabling direct offers to eligible Indonesian parties.
  • Introduces a 90-day response window for MEMR and permits the appointment of an independent appraiser.
  • Enables MEMR or regional governors to allocate shares among interested SOEs or ROEs.
  • Adds a due diligence process for Indonesian buyers, covering technical, financial, and legal aspects.
  • Permits the use of a special purpose vehicle (SPV) to facilitate divestment among multiple domestic entities.
Key provisions under MEMR 9/2017:
  • Establishes a gradual divestment schedule based on the number of years since the company entered the production stage:
    • Year 6: max 20% foreign ownership
    • Year 7: max 30%
    • Year 8: max 37%
    • Year 9: max 44%
    • Year 10: max 51%
  • Requires that the divestment share price be based on fair market value, excluding the valuation of mineral or coal reserves.
  • Sets a priority sequence for divestment offers: central government, then regional governments, state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and finally Indonesian private entities.

title: MEMR Regulation No. 25/2018 - Domestic Market Obligation (DMO)
description:
Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (MEMR) Regulation No. 25 of 2018 aims to ensure the domestic availability of coal and minerals, support national energy and economic resilience and stabilise commodity prices. It applies to both coal and mineral mining permit holders (production operation mining business licenses or IUP and special mining business licenses IUPK), including those involved in processing, refining, transportation and sales.

Key provisions include:
  • Mining companies must prioritise domestic demand before exporting.
  • The specific DMO levels (e.g., percentage of production allocated to domestic market) are not fixed in the regulation but are determined annually by the MEMR. 
  • MEMR may also regulate types and quantities of minerals required for domestic use.
To implement these provisions:
  • Annual MEMR decrees set DMO quotas and price caps (e.g., MEMR Decree No. 72.K/MB.01/MEM.B/2025 on the sale of metal minerals and coal). 
  • Export approvals are contingent on meeting DMO obligations.
While not a price regulation, this policy is complementary to Indonesia's metal domestic price regulation policies.
